statements.body: The choir owns hundreds of physical scores stored in a cupboard.
There are approximately forty members in the choir.
There is currently no catalog of the scores, so members cannot discover what the choir owns without asking the librarian.
The librarian currently acts as a human search engine for score discovery and borrowing, which is the pain point driving this project.
Scores are borrowed by members and the current state of who has what is not tracked systematically.
The project will build a score catalog with borrowing tracking functionality.
Who will administer the catalog day to day — the existing librarian, a designated member, or a self-service model?
What information should each score record contain — composer, arranger, publisher, voice-part breakdown, number of copies, condition, or other fields?
What happens when a score is not returned on time — is there a reminder or escalation process?
Reducing librarian interruptions is the primary success signal, implying the catalog must be self-service enough that members can find and request scores without librarian involvement.
Whether the system needs to support digital scores or attachments alongside physical copy tracking is not decided.

concerns.coverage: The librarian bears the full burden of score discovery and loan tracking for a forty-person choir with hundreds of scores; without the project, members must ask the librarian directly for every lookup and every borrow, making the role unsustainably manual.

The choir has approximately forty members who borrow scores, and at least one librarian role that currently handles all catalog and borrowing queries; no information yet on technical comfort level or how members typically communicate.

The idea names two workflow threads: (1) discovery — a member wants to know whether a score exists and where it is; (2) borrowing — a member takes a score and the system must record who has it and when it is due back. Entry and exit points for borrowing are implied but not detailed.

The system must hold records for hundreds of scores and track active loans per member; the required fields per score record and per loan record are not yet specified; nothing has been said about data retention, export, or backup expectations.
The librarian is the implied operator, but whether they administer the catalog or are relieved of that duty entirely is unknown; hosting, cost, and maintenance responsibilities are not addressed.

The idea implies success means the librarian stops being a human search engine, but no measurable threshold is stated — for example, reduction in direct librarian queries or percentage of borrows self-logged by members.

candidates.body: At the moment a member takes a score from the cupboard, how will the loan actually get recorded — on their own phone, a shared device by the cupboard, or by telling someone?
candidates.whySelected: The borrowing capture point is the heart of the first vertical slice and the biggest open workflow gap: if capture is not effortless at the cupboard, members will skip it and the loan ledger drifts back to the librarian's memory, defeating the stated success signal.

candidates.body: Who will enter the hundreds of existing scores into the catalog initially, and how much time can they realistically give it?
candidates.whySelected: Initial population is the largest single cost of the project and bounds the first slice's data model — a field set nobody has time to fill is a design error. It also tests whether the librarian's burden shifts rather than shrinks.

candidates.body: Does the librarian want to remain the catalog administrator, or is the goal to remove them from the loop entirely?
candidates.whySelected: This directly resolves the tension between the self-service success criterion and the still-open administration model, and it determines whether the design needs an admin role at all in the first slice.

contradictions.summary: Success is defined as members finding and requesting scores without librarian involvement, yet whether the librarian administers the catalog day to day is undecided — if administration falls back on the librarian, the interruption burden may be relocated rather than reduced.

readyAdvice.why: All ten core concerns have at least surface coverage, but the first vertical slice is not yet bounded: the borrowing capture mechanism, the initial data-entry path, and the administration model are all open, and any one of them could invalidate a build started today.

statements.body: The catalog must hold approximately 400 score titles.
Each title has between 10 and 50 physical copies, implying total physical copy count in the range of 4,000 to 20,000 items.
The minimum required fields per score record are: title, composer, arrangement, and copy count.
Scanning or attaching digital sheet music is explicitly out of scope for this project.

concerns.coverage: The corpus is approximately 400 titles with 10–50 copies each; required record fields are title, composer, arrangement, and copy count; digital attachments or scans are explicitly excluded from scope.
Digitising or attaching sheet music scans is a confirmed non-goal for this phase.

candidates.body: At the moment a member takes copies from the cupboard, how exactly do they record the borrow — a shared device by the cupboard, their own phone, a paper log later transcribed, or something else?
candidates.whySelected: Self-service borrowing is the primary success driver, but the capture point — the single moment where a loan becomes a record — is undefined. This is the riskiest unknown for the first vertical slice: if members can't or won't log borrows at the cupboard, the whole tracking premise fails regardless of catalog quality. Answering it bounds the slice's UI, hosting, and device assumptions in one stroke.

candidates.body: Who will administer the catalog day to day — the existing librarian, another designated member, or a fully self-service model with no administrator?
candidates.whySelected: This unknown is already recorded in the ledger but unanswered. It determines whether the design must include admin tooling in the first slice and whether the librarian's workload actually drops, which is the stated success signal.

candidates.body: What observable evidence, after one term of use, would tell you the project worked — for example, a specific reduction in questions to the librarian or a percentage of borrows logged by members themselves?
candidates.whySelected: Success coverage exists but names no measurable threshold. A concrete signal lets the first slice be judged rather than merely shipped, though it constrains the slice less directly than the capture-point question.

readyAdvice.why: Core concerns are nominally covered and scope is well bounded (400 titles, minimum fields, digital scans excluded), but the borrow-capture mechanism and the administrator role are still undecided. Both directly shape the first vertical slice, so at least one should be resolved before building begins.
